name: The Cedro-do-Bucaco of the Passo de Anas

location.address: Junto ao Passo de Anas, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

story:
Bucaco keeps two protected cypresses within sixty metres of each other on this path, and this is the smaller one: 3.68 metres round, 27 metres tall, with a crown nineteen metres across on the state's 2016 survey. In most forests that would be the headline tree. Here it is the fourth cypress on the hillside with a file of its own.

Its address is the Passo de Anas, a station on the Via Sacra named for the night Christ was taken before Annas the high priest. Barefoot Carmelite friars set these chapels out across the slope at the end of the seventeenth century and spaced them to match the distances of the walk through Jerusalem. That spacing still decides how people cross this forest. You do not go hunting for the cypress. You come round a bend expecting a shrine and find the tree standing over it.

Cupressus lusitanica came from the mountains of Mexico and Guatemala, and it has been planted inside these walls in such numbers, for so long, that most Portuguese take it for a native.

Nobody has dated this one and the register does not try. If you know how old it is, tell us.

access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
transport: On the Via Sacra path at the Passo de Anas station, about 60m from the Cedro-do-Bucaco of the Ermida do Sacramento (bsc_015)

name: The Cedro-do-Bucaco of the Casa de Guarda do Serpa
age_estimate: about 100 years, register figure, exact measurement date not recorded

location.address: Cerca de 200m a leste da Casa de Guarda do Serpa, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

story:
This is the thickest cypress in Bucaco's protected collection and, on the register's own figures, much the youngest of them. Four metres seventy-two around the trunk, thirty-five metres tall, and an age recorded as about a hundred years, against the three centuries the same register gives the cypress at the Via Sacra's first-fall station, a tree only half a metre wider.

Read that pairing carefully rather than as a marvel. The register does not say when the hundred years were counted, so the honest span is somewhere between ninety and a hundred and thirty, and a walled hillside laid out to make imported conifers grow fast is exactly where a cypress would put on girth quickly.

It stands about two hundred metres east of the Casa de Guarda do Serpa, the keeper's house at the northern edge of the forest, on a working track rather than a pilgrim path. This is where Bucaco's classified trees run out: the last entry before the collection gives way to ordinary hillside, and the quietest of the four cypresses on this page by some distance.

One more oddity worth carrying up there with you. The 2018 decree that classified the forest's other cypresses does not cover this one. It holds its place in the national register on its own paperwork, and nobody has written down why.

access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
transport: On a forest track about 200m east of the Casa de Guarda do Serpa gatehouse, at the north edge of the forest's classified-tree cluster

name: The Mexican White Pine of the Cova da Raposa
age_estimate: about 100 years, register figure, exact measurement date not recorded

location.address: Cova da Raposa, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

story:
Cova da Raposa means the fox's hollow, and what grows in it is a pine from the highlands of Mexico and Central America, forty metres of it.

Pinus ayacahuite has taken the height here and skipped the bulk. Forty metres tall on a trunk 2.55 metres round makes it taller than any of the four protected cypresses on this page and considerably narrower than all of them, a shape you notice from directly underneath: the crown starts a long way up and the trunk goes to it almost without a bend.

It belongs to the same imported collection as those cypresses, a hillside filled with conifers from four continents behind one wall and kept up since by the state that manages the forest now. A walk of twenty minutes here crosses more of the world's mountain ranges than most botanical gardens manage in a hectare.

The register gives its age as about a hundred years and records no date for that count, so the honest reading is somewhere between ninety and a hundred and thirty. Like the big cypress standing a short walk away by the Casa de Guarda do Serpa, it falls outside the 2018 decree that classified the forest's better known trees. It holds its protection on its own paperwork instead, which is a thinner kind of fame and no reason to walk past it.

access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
transport: At the Cova da Raposa, in the forest interior, close to the Cedro-do-Bucaco of the Casa de Guarda do Serpa (bsc_017)

name: The Magenta Cherry at the Forest Nursery

location.address: A entrada do viveiro florestal, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

verified_sources: https://si.icnf.pt/wfs/arv_class (ICNF national monumental trees register, processo AIP01110435I, girth 3.15m, crown 9.4m, measured 2016)
access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
transport: At the entrance to the forest's own tree nursery (viveiro florestal)
story:
At the entrance to Bucaco's own tree nursery stands a magenta cherry, an Australian rainforest species usually kept as a hedge or a garden specimen rather than left to become a trunk 3.15 metres round. The register measured that girth and a crown almost as wide, 9.4 metres, in 2016, and recorded neither a height nor an age for it, which for Syzygium paniculatum is nearly as unusual as the size itself.

Wild magenta cherry fruits a small sharp berry that gives the species its name, eaten straight off the branch or turned into jam in its native range, and it rarely grows this thick there. Two centuries of care for imported trees on this hillside, and a spot right beside the nursery that has propagated Bucaco's collection since the monks first planted it, seem to be what let this one keep going past the size most of its kind ever reach.

It is a plainer address than the shrines and squares nearby, a working entrance rather than a monument, which fits a tree that is really evidence the nursery's own methods work.

Nobody has dated it and the register does not try. If you know how old it is, tell us.
